claims: which parts of a block-level transition function apply effects that no transaction in the block requested
how a transition function as a mapping between states relates to code that updates one stored state in place
how a transition function differs from the virtual machine, execution environment and client that compute it
how a transition the rules permit differs from one its submitter or a contract's authors intended
when a sequence of transitions each valid on its own is not valid as a whole
how the invalidity of one transition carries over to the blocks and states built on top of it
who is exposed when participants that do not check validity themselves accept an invalid transition
how a design can rule out some invalid transitions by construction rather than by a check at each transition
which party states each precondition of a transition and how submitter-set conditions differ from those set by the protocol or held in state
how a precondition differs from an invariant and from a postcondition of the same transition
how preconditions on time or chain position differ from preconditions on state entries in how their truth can change
how effects written as absolute values differ from effects written as relative changes in what they assume about the pre-state
whether a transition's effects can be known before it executes or only discovered by executing it
how effects that create or remove state entries differ in lasting cost from effects that update existing entries
how a protocol sets the unit whose effects apply indivisibly, from a single transaction up to a whole block or batch
how a node keeps its persisted state at one defined position when applying a transition is interrupted
how the atomicity of a transition relates to its later reversal as a whole by a reorganization or rollback

audit.note: Re-audit after repair cycle 1 (auditor A, scoped; not expanded: the repair narrowed sentences at their own scope and changed no argument, assumption, structure or territory). Advisory: (a) B-B3, deferred by human decision: the accepted parent transitions record says without condition that a block's transition is the composition of its transactions' transitions; this record's block-level-steps claim is correct, so the parent should be scoped in a later maintenance change. (b) body[6] lists the block-level steps among 'steps no instruction performs', but Ethereum's beacon-root write (body[0]) is a system call that runs the system contract's EVM code; 'steps no transaction's code performs' would be more exact. audit.note: Signal-only audit (fresh auditor) of neighbour-overlap:4e0df4d60c against unchanged records valid-transitions 571753b74b13 and invalid-transitions 38a097a3b6f5; prior re-audit note follows. Re-audit A after repair cycle 1 (simplified v1), scoped to the change in diffs/valid-transitions-c1.diff (before 6e4f5862..., after 571753b7...); not expanded to a full audit, since the repair changed one case definition and two closing sentences without changing the record's structure, scope or claims. Re-read paragraphs 4 to 8 in full, the definition and every use of 'state' (definition, paragraphs 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8) against the accepted state, global-state, transition-rules, rules and transaction-validation records and the sibling transition-functions. B-B2 resolved: paragraph 4 now says adoption settles which rules a participant runs and a check settles validity under them; the attacker's transactions precede the fork height and are valid under both rule sets, while the one-time balance move at that height is valid only under the forked rules (a non-adopting node rejects that block's state result); this agrees with rules (a validating participant applies validity rules itself), transition-rules (outer-rule changes at an agreed height) and transition-functions (the DAO fork as a one-time change at its activation height). B-B1 resolved: paragraph 5's second case is now defined by the single-transition conditions each member meets at its position, so 'state' no longer carries a protocol-state sense there; Bitcoin's block weight (checked over the assembled block) and Ethereum's block gas bound both fit it. Paragraph 7's new sentence says carrying the running total makes the condition over the sequence one each member meets or fails in the state it meets, so the transaction that no longer fits is invalid at its position; this matches the definition ('accepted in the state it meets'), the State record's state-machine sense, global-state (values consulted by later transitions are state in that sense without being global-state entries) and transaction-validation (in Ethereum a block whose member fails validity at its position is rejected whole), and paragraph 6's 'its acceptable members included' still holds. Paragraph 8 ('where the rules state no condition over the sequence') is consistent with the recast condition, which the rules still state. Every remaining use of 'state' now has the state-machine sense or a qualified compound ('account state', 'contract's state'). Overlap: one placement (State Transitions); the changed sentences restate no parent sentence. Territory: the new sentences name no further concept and explain neither Hard Forks nor Block Validation. Representation unchanged and still fitting. Canonical: no positional or dated words, American English, plain text. Repair-introduced blocking defects: none. Advisory: (1) Deferred by human decision: the parent's sentence 'a block's transition is the composition of its transactions' transitions in order' omits block-level steps. (2) Paragraph 7's 'although it meets every condition about a single transition' could be read as including the recast per-member condition it just introduced; 'every condition about that transition alone' would remove the doubt. (3) Paragraph 7's new sentence partly repeats the earlier 'identified when it is reached' and 'finds the transaction that no longer fits when it reaches it'. (4) The stolen-key example in paragraph 1 shows a gap with the key holder's intention, not the submitter's. (5) Paragraph 8's 'takes a rule that consults a running total' is narrower than needed; a record of earlier withdrawals suffices. (6) The swap example (paragraph 2) and the DAO mechanism (paragraph 3) paraphrase Sandwich Attacks and Reentrancy without naming them. (7) Paragraph 4's 'Because validity reads nothing beyond the rules' is looser than paragraph 1's rules, input and state. (8) 'a node that refused such a transition' relies on refusing meaning judging invalid. (9) 'without any mistake by the submitter' sits uneasily beside 'a loosely set minimum output'. (10) 'unprotected initialization function' simplifies Parity's case (the library itself had never been initialized). (11) A failed submitter-set minimum output makes an Ethereum transaction revert while it stays valid at protocol level; the record makes no false claim but does not mark the two layers.

The shared wording is the complementary condition only: valid-transitions defines validity as the input accepted in the state it meets and the produced state being the one the rules assign; invalid-transitions defines its negation (input refused, or a resulting state that differs), the correct complement of that conjunction, contradicting nothing. The bodies split cleanly: valid-transitions explains what the check reads, the gap between permitted and intended (submitter, ordering, contract authors, remedies) and conditions over sequences; invalid-transitions explains what follows when validity fails (history-relative acceptability, carry-over from transaction to block to descendants, unchecked acceptance and its consequences, exclusion by construction). Where both touch block-level effects they agree (valid: a block violating an aggregate bound is invalid with its acceptable members; invalid: a member failing at its position carries invalidity to its block in Ethereum and Bitcoin, not where rules skip it) and hand off to Block Validation or Transaction Validation; neither re-explains the other's responsibility.

audit.note: Re-audit after repair cycle 1 (auditor A), expanded to a complete audit because the repair changed the opening argument (state reachability reframed as history validity) and the flow. Resolved: (1) the opening paragraph now states invalidity of histories and says the left state is often, not necessarily, unreachable, with a fitting existence example (an unsigned transfer leaving the state a signed one would); the flow's unchecked stage reads 'a state reached through an invalid history'; later uses ('can show it a state no valid history reaches', 'not that a valid history reaches it') are hedged or negative and stay true; consistent with State (histories ending in the same state are interchangeable for later rules; snapshots covered only if reachable). (2) The flow label is scoped to designs that refuse the block, matching the conditioned paragraph and Transaction Validation's skip designs. (3) Divergence is now 'at least in the entries the transition left with values the rules would not have given them', true for both kinds of invalidity in the definition. (4) The lead of the construction paragraph ('no check, at the transition, of the property they would break') fits route one (local balance checks remain, the total is never computed) and route two; 'execution needs no check for duplication' holds even where a VM repeats ability checks defensively; the closing sentence is conditioned on nothing at the transition repeating what was shown once. (5) Non-checking participants exclude validity-proof verifiers, consistent with Global State's comparison (stateless validators execute, light clients check headers only). The cut work-weighted sentence carried nothing the paragraph relied on: the light-client sentence and 'That takes producers or signers who accepted it' stand without it. Overlap per placement (one placement): no restatement of State Transitions' sentences; the deferred parent omission of block-level steps is not counted. Territory and splits: excluded concepts (Reorganizations, Transaction Validation, Light Nodes, Fraud Proofs, Rules, Inputs) are named only; no leakage into Valid Transitions (permitted vs intended, sequence conditions) or Transition Functions (block-level steps named only); checked against Transition Rules and Transaction Reversion with no contradiction. Representation: the scoped flow shows the branch by whether a participant checks; prose carries the rest. Accuracy and depth: every sentence re-read; no depth-long signal; depth follows the three claims. Advisory: (a) opening paragraph, 'since the state records no signatures' reads as universal; 'where the state records no signatures' would scope it, since some designs keep processed signatures for replay protection (Solana, per Transaction Reversion); the example itself holds as an existence claim. (b) 'a branch that runs from the invalid block's parent' and the flow stage 'Valid branch followed from the parent': the best valid branch can fork below the parent. (c) Definition 'the one the rules assign' assumes deterministic rules (Transition Rules allows open choices); group-level wording shared with Valid Transitions. (d) 'refuse it when any of its transactions fails at its position' could say 'fails a validity rule' so it cannot be read as reverting. (e) Closing 'wherever they are attempted' leaves the contrast with a single missing check implicit. (f) The flow's 'Accepted unchecked' branch does not name the faulty-implementation case the next paragraph includes.

audit.note: Re-audit (auditor A) after repair cycle 1, scoped to the c1 word diff (06d7096f -> 879e2c47), which touches paragraphs 6 and 7 only; not expanded, since the repair narrowed two claims and re-anchored one lead sentence without changing the argument, its assumptions, the structure or the scope. Resolved: A-B1 = B-B1, the monotonicity result is now limited to a condition comparing a never-decreasing measure with one fixed point, with a two-sided window stated as one of each and changing truth at most twice; on a non-decreasing measure a window's truth runs false, true, false at most (zero changes if the measure jumps past it), so 'at most twice' is exact, and the following 'an expired input cannot become acceptable again' still holds since it concerns the upper bound. B-B2, the producer-timestamp clause is scoped to designs that judge time conditions against a timestamp the producer sets for that block, and Bitcoin is correctly placed: under BIP 113 lock times are measured against the median of the eleven earlier timestamps, so a block's own timestamp feeds only the median later blocks use; 'one height and one time fixed for the block' is now true of both Bitcoin and Ethereum. Determinism cross-record: the lead now says a block's own height and timestamp are carried with its transactions and values earlier blocks left (a median of their timestamps) are state, which matches Determinism's block-timestamp-as-input example and State's definition (what the rules consult with the next input). Checked the changed sentences, their paragraphs and dependent claims against determinism, inputs, state, transaction-validation (position-dependent checks against the including block, drift between signing and position: consistent), transaction-reversion (no time claims touched), transition-functions (values the block carries, position and queues in state feed the block: consistent), valid-transitions and invalid-transitions (no conflict). Parent overlap at the one placement (State & Data / State Transitions / Transition Preconditions): none introduced. Territory: Timelocks and Validity Windows still only named; no sibling label explained. Representation unchanged (one distinction, prose elsewhere). Canonical validity: no positional or dated words introduced; American English. Depth: 1339 words, see the depth-long resolution. Advisory: (1) 'a condition that compares it with one fixed point' literally includes equality with one height, which changes truth twice; 'with one threshold' would be exact, though the colon's two one-sided cases make the intended reading clear; (2) 'in Bitcoin its timestamp counts only toward the median later blocks are measured against' is scoped to time conditions by its sentence, but Bitcoin timestamps also feed difficulty retargeting, so 'for time conditions' would make the scope explicit; (3) 'values earlier blocks left in the state, such as a median of their timestamps': the median is computed from timestamps earlier blocks left rather than itself left; (4) known and deferred by human decision: the parent's composition sentence omits block-level steps; (5) paragraph 2's 'What it states applies on top of the other conditions. It narrows ...' partly repeats paragraph 1's 'those bind that input alone'; (6) 'Whoever put such an entry there stated the condition': for a Bitcoin output the recipient usually chooses the locking conditions the payer writes; (7) 'a precondition that can be evaluated only by computing the effects' is strong where a swap's output can be computed ahead; 'evaluated, as written, by computing the effects' would soften it; (8) 'that a signature verifies' could read 'that the signing key is one the state authorizes' to match Inputs' split, not a contradiction as written.

audit.note: Re-audit after repair cycle 1 (auditor A), expanded into a complete audit because the definition changed and a paragraph was removed. Evidence: diff WORK/diffs/atomic-state-transitions-c1.diff (before 9f91e499..., after 3610cbca...). Findings answered: (1) the definition is now relative to the participant that adopts state by the unit ('drawn by the rules a participant applies ... whose effects that participant adopts together or not at all'); checked against every paragraph: paragraph 1 (protocol rules draw the unit by failure handling; the payload and block units in Ethereum, the skip design), paragraph 2 (a validating node adopts the block's result only after the whole block passes), paragraph 3 (the settlement contract adopts by batch while rollup nodes adopt by block, so the closing sentence now follows from the definition instead of contradicting it), paragraphs 4 to 6 (a node following the rules does not resume from a mixed store), paragraph 7 (reversal removes whole units and every later unit, matching 'applies no later unit on top of one'). Resolved. (2) The lead now says clients make sure, before the node resumes from its store, that the entries are the state at one position and the store names it; this holds for the single atomic write and for both recovery examples, and agrees with 'need a recovery procedure instead'. Resolved. (3) Bitcoin Core's recovery is now a replay to the newer block, undoing the older branch's blocks back to the fork point only when the flush spanned a branch switch; this matches ReplayBlocks (head-blocks marker written first, rollback of the old branch to the common ancestor, idempotent roll-forward), and the idempotence clause holds for both steps. Resolved. (4) 'rollback' now appears once, scoped generically as 'a rollback that returns a chain to an earlier height', and the reversal is attributed to Reorganizations only; no sentence is attributed to the Rollbacks execution-recovery concept, so no contradiction with Partial Failures' or Execution Recovery's use remains. Resolved. (5) The final paragraph (re-inclusion, conflicting spends, off-chain effects) is cut; nothing remaining depended on it, claim 3 is still answered by the reversal paragraph, and the overlaps with Partial Failures, Reorganizations and Invalid Transitions it carried are gone. Resolved. Overlap per placement (one placement, State & Data / State Transitions): no sentence restates the parent's definition ('applying all of its effects together'), its composition paragraph or its closing paragraph; the definition is now further from the domain sentence. Territory and splits: claims 1 (paragraphs 1 to 3), 2 (paragraphs 4 to 6) and 3 (paragraph 7) each explained; excluded concepts named, not explained; consistent with Transaction Atomicity (payload unit, fee and sequence number outside it, journals and buffers in memory), Transaction Validation (block invalid in Ethereum, skip in some rollups), Global State (positions inside a block, branch switch returns to the common ancestor), State, Atomicity Guarantees, Partial Failures and the five siblings (Transition Functions defers interruption to this concept; Invalid Transitions' carry-over is a different angle). Representation: all prose, suited to argument and conditioned examples; no structure missing or unneeded. Accuracy and depth: 1,145 words across three claims; Ethereum failed-transaction inclusion and withdrawal credits, Bitcoin Core's temporary coins view and partial flushes, go-ethereum's periodic persistence and head rewind, the validity-proof batch example and the write-caching caveat all checked; American English; no positional or dated words. Advisory: (a) repair-introduced, non-material: 'replays the blocks from the older block to the newer one, first undoing ... back to where the branches meet' leaves the replay's start loosely stated after a branch switch, where it runs from the meeting point; 'replays the blocks up to the newer one' would be exact. (b) Paragraph 3's 'The unit is therefore fixed by who adopts the state as well as by the rules' now partly repeats the participant-relative definition; it reads as the example's consequence. (c) 'How the reversal itself is carried out belongs to Reorganizations' follows a sentence that also names a chain rollback; acceptable since such a rollback returns the chain to an earlier block as a reorganization does. (d) Pre-existing: 'the stored entries are the state at one position' is loose for stores that also keep other states' nodes, such as hash-keyed tries; 'hold the state' would be exact. (e) Pre-existing: 'a combination that is the state at no position' and 'matches no position' could read 'need not be'. (f) Pre-existing: 'The states after each transaction exist while the block is computed' is close to the parent's intermediate-states sentence. (g) Pre-existing: the validity-failure block sentence sits near Invalid Transitions' carry-over, from a different angle. (h) Pre-existing: 'an execution failure' borrows the Execution Failures concept's words in the transaction sense. (i) Pre-existing: paragraph 2's fee-paid nesting point echoes paragraph 1's Ethereum inclusion point. (j) Known and deferred by human decision: the parent's composition sentence omits block-level steps; the record's unrequested-steps sentence adds to it without contradicting it.

groupAudit.note: Group audit, simplified pipeline v1: the six owned members read side by side and against transitions, transition-rules, inputs, determinism, state, global-state, transaction-validation, transaction-reversion, transaction-atomicity, transaction-execution, atomicity-guarantees and partial-failures. No contradiction between members or with those neighbours: the whole-block refusal of a transaction failing a validity rule (Ethereum, Bitcoin) versus rollups that skip it, the fee and sequence-number update surviving a payload failure, positions inside a block, the block's height and timestamp carried with the input, and refusal leaving the state as it was are stated alike wherever they recur. Each member keeps to its labels and names the others only to draw boundaries (valid-transitions to Transition Preconditions for submitter conditions, transition-effects to Transition Preconditions for bounds, transition-functions to Atomic State Transitions for interruption, atomic-state-transitions to Transition Functions for unrequested steps). No member explains state roots or commitments: invalid-transitions says only what a proof against a header's commitment establishes, atomic-state-transitions names a rollup's state root as the thing a settlement contract adopts. State is used consistently: valid-transitions marks its running gas total as state in the state-machine sense and not an account-state entry, in line with global-state; the other members use the protocol's state at a position or the stored entries. Convergence: the definition openings follow the concept titles; forms differ (three distinction chains over different conflations, each answering a claim phrased as a difference, one flow, two prose records); the point that an input meets the state its predecessors left recurs in valid-transitions, transition-preconditions and transition-effects, each for its own claim (unintended outcomes, how a condition's truth changes, effects unknowable before execution), which is repetition that follows the claims, not convergence. Advisory: (1) known and deferred by human decision: the parent's sentence that a block's transition is the composition of its transactions' transitions omits the block-level steps transition-functions describes; a maintenance change will correct the parent. (2) transition-preconditions, 'or values earlier blocks left in the state, such as a median of their timestamps': this is state in the state-machine sense, which the record's definition needs, but Bitcoin reads that median from recent headers rather than from its unspent set; marking the sense, as valid-transitions does, would keep a reader of global-state from seeing a conflict. (3) invalid-transitions and atomic-state-transitions both state the Ethereum and Bitcoin whole-block refusal against the rollup skip, each citing Transaction Validation; divided by angle (carry-over of invalidity versus where the atomic unit lies), minor redundancy. (4) transition-functions' clause on hash-addressed trees keeping an earlier state readable under its old root is the nearest any member comes to state-commitments territory; it describes storage reuse, not what a root commits to, and is worth rechecking when that group is authored.

resolutions.resolution: Not a defect. The 38% overlap between valid-transitions and invalid-transitions comes from their complementary definitions, which must use the same terms (rules in force, the input accepted or refused in the state it meets, the state the rules assign) to agree with each other, and they do. The bodies take different claims: valid-transitions the gap between permitted and intended and conditions over a sequence; invalid-transitions the carry-over of invalidity to descendants, who is exposed when checks are delegated, and exclusion by construction. No argument or example is made in both.

Not convergence. valid-transitions, invalid-transitions and atomic-state-transitions open with 'A valid transition is', 'An invalid transition is' and 'An atomic state transition is' because their titles end in 'transition' and the definition leads every record; the opening follows the labels. The definitions then diverge in content, and the bodies differ in arc and form (distinction then prose, prose with a flow, prose only).
